title: How teachers can help or hinder learning -1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton opens his series on teaching, the eleventh of his twelve factors affecting learning, by describing the realities of the job: it is hard, bad teaching is in some respects harder than good teaching, and no teaching is easy. He argues for a good-enough standard borrowed from Winnicott's thinking on parents, since most of the large teaching workforce sits between outstanding and shocking. The post then names what he sees as the most radical change in teaching that a learning focus produces: teachers cease to be the stars and become the roadies, with the students as the band. He explains that teachers work hard before the gig and should work equally hard in a different way, and he criticises school social media that praises amazing teachers without evidence of learning.
points: Bad teaching is paradoxically harder than good teaching because it generates misbehaviour, exhaustion and tension in a cycle.
A good-enough standard fits a profession of hundreds of thousands of people, only a few of whom are outstanding or shocking.
The biggest shift a learning focus brings is that the teacher stops being the star and becomes the roadie.
Teachers and students should work equally hard, but at different times and tasks, so the idea that teachers must never out-work students is wrong.
quotes: Oddly, bad teaching is less easy than good teaching. Bad teaching is an enabler of student misbehaviour, disinterest and/or boredom, of colleagues’ irritation, of parental concern, of bad learning and of increased monitoring by school leaders. Bad teaching makes teachers exhausted, self-conscious and unhappy, enables those dissatisfactions to be taken home with them and then creates family tensions which are brought back into school to start the cycle all over again.
There are truly outstanding teachers; I have worked with just one of those in my entire career. There are some truly shocking teachers; I once worked with two of those in the same school.

Teaching is simply one of the most rewarding jobs in the world if you are lucky enough to be in a place where - academic, social, emotional and physical - learning happens. Being in a classroom or around a school when a child or student makes a breakthrough in their current learning struggle is nothing else other than thrilling, especially so if you know that your thought and preparation last evening was the trigger for the improvement.

Establishing learning as the Hedgehog Concept of schools and classrooms has radically upended all that in a way that some teachers are still struggling to come to terms with. Probably the single biggest change in the nature of teaching is that the learning-focused teacher is no longer the star of the show but is now a very important roadie.

If learning - children and students actually getting better - is at the very heart of a learning-focused school then their performance - academic, social, emotional and physical - is what matters most. That’s what the audience wants to see. That’s what the stomping applause should be given for.

But this idea isn’t true generally. By the time the band came on stage at the gig I went to, the roadies had already worked super hard on their behalf. By the time children and students arrive for their learning gig, the teachers will already have worked super-hard to make sure that everything is ready for the learning band to shine. Teachers and students should work equally hard, at different times and at different things.

The spotlight in truly learning-focused schools shines differently now. It shines first on the children and students who are going through hopefully good struggles and learning and then on the teacher roadies who have helped them.
